extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and graduate students in mass communication/journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Conceptual and empirical criteria for how internal and external forces influence news content—covering staff-size and management pressures, agenda building/setting, frame building/setting, and agenda cutting. Useful for researchers designing studies of media influence or evaluating news coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-media organization factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on forces within the news entity that may affect how journalists produce content and cover (or not cover) certain topics — e.g., pressure from management (assignment editors or other superiors) and smaller-scale organizational restraints such as staff size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centers on possible management pressure and organizational constraints operating inside the news organization; these internal influences are distinct from extramedia or elite sources and are discussed as a separate level in hierarchical models of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff size pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff size of a media organization is linked to ownership, competition, news quality, and industry performance; findings typically indicate that a larger staff size is most desirable for quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: reductions in staff were associated with perceived declines in quality; larger news budgets and staff generally correspond to higher quality programming. Counterexamples: larger stations sometimes devote a smaller percentage of space to local news despite longer newscasts (stations may expand hours rather than staff). Survey evidence on staff trends can conflict across studies and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct management pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Overt managerial actions or communications that explicitly tell journalists not to cover a story or give clear instructions about what topics to cover (or not) and how to cover them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include superiors specifically telling reporters not to cover an item or issuing explicit editorial instructions. Survey data: among journalists who believed avoidance occurred, substantial shares reported 'direct signals' such as being told not to cover stories or that types of stories were unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect management pressures (socialization/unwritten codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtle, informal means of control in newsrooms where newsroom routines, editing, reprimands, or unspoken signals socialize journalists to learn what is acceptable—'learned by osmosis' or as reflexive unwritten codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifestations include yawning at a pitch, not airing a produced story, nods of disapproval; these hidden norms are powerful but harder to define, measure, and analyze than explicit policy. Scholars note unwritten ethics and reflexes often guide decision making more than formal codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence modes on media content (three outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: External and internal sources may shape coverage by: (1) affecting the topics/stories the media cover (building the media's agenda); (2) influencing how a story is covered (the angle or tone — building media frames); or (3) convincing the media to give an issue little attention or not to cover it at all (cutting the item from the media's agenda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framework (agenda building, frame building, agenda cutting) to classify types of influence and design studies examining either what gets coverage, how it is presented, or what is omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda building (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process by which internal and external forces tell the media what to think (and write) about — i.e., forces that attempt to set the media agenda (media agenda as dependent variable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different from agenda setting (media -> audience). Historical notes: developed alongside and distinct from agenda-setting scholarship. Use models (e.g., Shoemaker & Reese 'onion diagram') to locate levels of influence (elites, organizational, extramedia, within-media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda setting vs. agenda building distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda setting concerns how media influence public salience (media agenda as independent variable); agenda building focuses on how outside/inside forces set the media agenda (media agenda as dependent variable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two processes are connected but analytically distinct; naming conventions matter because operational variables and research designs differ. Figure/adaptations (Scheufele) illustrate ordering: influences -> media agenda -> audience agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame building (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes by which internal and external sources attempt to control or influence the way a story is covered — i.e., telling the media how to think/write about an issue (the angle, tone, or 'spin').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames are 'central organizing ideas' that provide meaning to events and can be deliberate or inadvertent; framing research must consider both the communicative source (e.g., advertiser) and intentions. Distinguish media frames (textual) from audience frames (cognitive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing conceptual clarity and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing is hard to study because of vague definitions and misuse of terms; researchers must specify frames as schemes for presenting and comprehending news and distinguish media frames from audience frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying framing effects (media frame -> audience frame), the recommended method is combining content analysis with survey data. When studying frame building (what influences media frames), focus on extramedia/organizational/within-media factors as independent variables. Scholars note lack of systematic evidence about how factors impact news framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda cutting (definition and modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phenomenon of keeping an item off the news agenda — described as (1) placing an item low on the agenda (burying it); (2) removing it from the agenda once it is there; or (3) never placing it on the agenda in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda cutting has been less studied; consequences include reducing public awareness (example: mad cow disease coverage correlated with consumer behavior). Use content analysis and case studies to document cutting. Project Censored and Media Tenor provide examples/approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for agenda cutting — logistical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur due to logistical constraints such as limited news hole and limited reporting staff; selection can be inadvertent or fortuitous rather than deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McCombs notes selection is often an inadvertent outcome of reporting; staff and space limits can force elimination of topics. Researchers should consider structural resource constraints when attributing omission to deliberate cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for agenda cutting — internal and external influences
rubrics_metrics.description: People within or outside the news organization may actively hide or camouflage stories to keep them off the agenda (e.g., executives deliberately burying unfavorable material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative evidence: internal emails instructing burying of stories; studies (Price, Colistra) showing organizations that would benefit from policy outcomes ignoring related coverage. Use archival documents, comparative outlet analysis, and longitudinal content measures to detect such influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution: paucity and measurement challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame-building and agenda-cutting research suffer from definitional vagueness and lack of systematic data; scholars note 'no evidence has yet been systematically collected' about how various factors impact structural qualities of news in terms of framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers are urged to develop clearer operationalizations, specify independent/dependent variables, combine methods (content analysis, surveys, longitudinal consumption/behavioral data), and expand empirical attention to these under-researched phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of influence levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences on media content can be classified at multiple levels: elites, organizational influences, extramedia influences, and within-media influences (including internal executives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hierarchical or 'onion' models (e.g., Shoemaker & Reese) to situate where pressures originate and to structure analyses that test how each level contributes to agenda-building, framing, or cutting.
